title: Heracles' Wars on Elis, Pylos and Sparta

summary.text: Cheated of his wage by Augeas, Heracles made war on Elis: the twin Moliones routed his first army, so he ambushed them at Cleonae, took the city and held the Olympic games, honouring Pelops. He then sacked Neleus' Pylos, where the shape-shifter Periclymenus fought him and Hades took an arrow for the defenders, and at Sparta destroyed Hippocoon's house and gave the throne back to Tyndareus.

chapters.title: The twin generals
chapters.text: Cheated by Augeas of his wage for cleansing the cattle-yards, Heracles came against Elis with an Arcadian army and volunteers from the champions of Greece. Augeas, who had made ready for the reckoning, gave the command to Eurytus and Cteatus, the Moliones — sons of his brother Actor and of Molione, though Poseidon too was called their father. Apollodorus says the two had grown together into one body and were the strongest men of their day; Homer's Nestor remembers them sharing one chariot, one at the reins and the other plying the whip. Heracles fell sick on the march and made a truce; learning of it, the twins fell on his army and killed many, and he withdrew. While Actor's sons were in their prime, Pausanias says, the war won the hero no glory.

chapters.title: Ambush at Cleonae
chapters.text: Heracles struck when the Isthmian festival came round. The Eleans sent the Moliones to share in the sacrifices — as sacred envoys under the Isthmian truce, in Pausanias — and at Cleonae, between Corinth and Argos, Heracles lay in wait and shot them down; Pausanias saw their tomb there. At first no one knew the killer. Their mother Molione hunted him out, and when he proved to be Heracles, then living at Tiryns, the Eleans demanded redress from Argos and, refused, begged Corinth to shut every Argive out of the Isthmian games. When that failed too, Molione cursed any Elean who would not stay away from the festival — and in Pausanias' day the athletes of Elis still kept away from the Isthmus.

chapters.title: Elis and Olympia
chapters.text: Heracles marched on Elis and took it. Apollodorus says he put Augeas and his sons to death and gave the kingdom to Phyleus, brought back from exile; in Pausanias he spared Augeas for Phyleus' sake, and the king lived on into old age — the Eleans honour him still as a hero — while Phyleus set the realm in order and went home to Dulichium. At Olympia the victor honoured his ancestor Pelops. Apollodorus has him found Pelops' altar and six altars for the twelve gods and hold the Olympic games; Pausanias knew the precinct Heracles set apart for Pelops, and the victors of his games — Iolaus in the chariot race with Heracles' own mares, Polydeuces at boxing, and Heracles himself in the wrestling and the pancratium. Hyginus too has him found contests at Olympia in Pelops' honour.

chapters.title: The sack of Pylos
chapters.text: From Elis Heracles turned on Pylos. Neleus had once refused to cleanse him of blood — Iphitus' blood, in Apollodorus; Megara's and her children's, in Hyginus, who makes that refusal the cause of the war. Apollodorus says Heracles took the city and killed Neleus and all his sons but Nestor, a youth then being reared among the Gerenians. Homer's Nestor remembers only that Heracles crushed Pylos and left him the last of Neleus' twelve sons — yet in his tale Neleus still reigns. Hades himself fought for the Pylians and took Heracles' arrow in the shoulder, climbing to Olympus to be healed. The Eleans told Pausanias it happened at their own Pylos, with Athena at Heracles' side — and that is why they alone of men honour Hades.

chapters.title: The shape-shifter
chapters.text: Bravest of Neleus' sons was Periclymenus, to whom Poseidon had given the power to change his shape — into whatever he prayed for in the press of battle, says Apollonius, who sets him on the Argo. Apollodorus has him fight Heracles now as a lion, now a snake, now a bee, and die with his brothers all the same. Ovid lets Nestor tell it at Troy, grudgingly, to Heracles' son Tlepolemus: having tried every form in vain, Periclymenus became the eagle that bears Jupiter's thunderbolts and raked the hero's face, until the Tirynthian's arrow caught him among the clouds where wing meets flank; he fell, and his own weight drove the shaft out through his throat. Hyginus alone lets him escape: his grandfather Neptune turned him into an eagle, and he flew from the siege alive.

chapters.title: The sons of Hippocoon
chapters.text: From Pylos Heracles marched on Sparta, where Hippocoon and his sons had driven out Tyndareus. He hated them for fighting beside Neleus, and still more for clubbing to death Licymnius' son — Oeonus, in Pausanias — who had struck their hound with a stone when it rushed at him; the Spartans said the feud began earlier, when the house refused to purify him of Iphitus' death. To win Cepheus of Tegea and his twenty sons for the war, Heracles gave Cepheus' daughter Sterope a lock of the Gorgon's hair, Athena's gift, to rout any army that came against the walls. Cepheus fell with all his sons, and Apollodorus adds Iphicles, the hero's own brother — though Pausanias records Iphicles' tomb at Pheneus, where he died of a wound the Moliones gave him. Heracles killed Hippocoon and his sons and gave the kingdom back to Tyndareus — in trust, the Heraclids would later claim.
